task_title: Runway Safety: Incursions, Excursions and Overruns
area: Area VI. Safety and Risk Management
objective: By the end of this lesson you can run a single-pilot taxi routine that keeps you off runways you are not cleared onto, work out a realistic landing distance for a wet or contaminated runway, and decide early and firmly whether to land or go around.
why: Accident statistics show a pilot is more at risk during approach and landing than in any other phase of flight [[24:209|AFH 9-38]]. FAA data cited in the PHAK say about 65 percent of runway incursions are caused by pilots, and almost half of those by general aviation pilots [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. Landing overruns add about ten incidents or accidents a year [[27:5|AC 91-79B 1.5.5]], and the unstabilized approach heads the FAA's list of overrun hazards [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.1]].

warmup: Think first: You are flying a Piper Archer to a 3,400 ft runway in light rain. The tower offers a closer runway with a 10 knot tailwind to save you a few minutes, and you are already a little high and fast. At what point should you have decided to say "unable" or go around, and what will make that decision hard in the moment?

key_terms.def: Any event on an airport where an aircraft, vehicle, person or object on the ground creates a collision hazard or loss of separation with an aircraft taking off, landing or intending to land.
An aircraft passing beyond the end of the runway during an aborted takeoff or on the landing rollout. One kind of runway excursion.
A place on the airport movement area with a history of potential collision or runway incursion, marked on airport diagrams with a brown circle or ellipse and a number (HS 1).
An ATC instruction to taxi onto the departure runway, line up and wait. It is not a takeoff clearance.
No unnecessary talk from passengers during taxi, takeoff, approach and landing, so the pilot can concentrate.
A constant-angle glide path to a chosen aiming point, at a constant airspeed and in the landing configuration, with only small corrections.
Ending an approach or landing and climbing away. A normal maneuver, not a failure.
The runway length declared usable for landing. A displaced threshold shortens it.
A check, made before descent, that you can land on the runway in use under the conditions reported then, with a safety margin.
A number from 6 (dry) down to 1 (poor), with 0 for nil, given by the airport for each third of the runway.
A pilot's report, in words (good, medium, poor, nil and steps between), of how well the wheel brakes stopped the airplane.
Tires riding on a wedge of water instead of the runway, so braking and steering are nearly lost.

chunks.title: Runway incursions and the single pilot

body.p: The AFH defines a runway incursion as any occurrence at an airport where an aircraft, vehicle, person or object on the ground creates a collision hazard or causes a loss of separation with an aircraft taking off, landing or intending to land [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. AC 91-73B quotes the FAA order wording: the incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle or person on the protected area of a surface meant for landing and takeoff [[7:1|AC 91-73B 1]].

Pilots are the biggest part of the problem. FAA data cited in the PHAK put about 65 percent of runway incursions on pilots, and almost half of those on GA pilots [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. The PHAK also says about three runway incursions happen each day at towered U.S. airports [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]]. Neither page gives a year for these numbers.

The AFH names three areas that contribute most: communications with ATC, airport knowledge, and flight deck procedures for keeping oriented [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. Investigations summarized in the PHAK found the same pattern: not complying with ATC instructions, not knowing the airport, and not following standard operating procedures [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

AC 91-73B is the FAA's guide for single-pilot Part 91 and Part 135 taxi procedures. It groups them into seven areas: planning, situational awareness, written taxi instructions, pilot and passenger communication, ATC and pilot communication, taxiing, and exterior lighting [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7a]]. Its goal is procedures that raise your awareness without adding to your workload while the airplane is moving [[7:2|AC 91-73B 5b]].

callout.text: AC 91-73B asks that these SOPs be evaluated during the flight review of every certificated pilot [[7:3|AC 91-73B 6]]. Application: expect your CFI to watch your taxi, not just your landings.

check.q: What three areas does the AFH say contribute most to runway incursions?
check.a: Communications with ATC, airport knowledge, and flight deck procedures for maintaining orientation [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

chunks.title: Plan and brief the taxi before you move

body.p: AC 91-73B treats moving on the airport as a phase of flight you plan like any other, in two parts: review items and briefing items [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b]].

bullets: Review NOTAMs and the ATIS for runway and taxiway closures and construction. If ATC clears you onto a surface the NOTAM or ATIS says is closed, query the controller [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b(1)(c)]].

Review the airport diagram, its hot spots and any published standard taxi routes for the big picture [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b(1)(d)]]. A hot spot is a place with a history of potential collision or runway incursion risk [[34:358|AIM PCG H-3]], drawn on the diagram as a brown open circle or ellipse with a number such as HS 1 [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide, Hot Spots]].

Brief the expected route, including hold short lines, runways to cross, hot spots and other conflicts [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(d)]]. Brief it before taxi and again before the descent to land, when it is fresh [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b(2)]].

Plan when you will run checklists and talk on the radio so they do not compete with watching where you are. If possible, run checklists only when stopped or on a straight taxiway with no complex intersections [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]].
Do as much as you can before you start rolling: flaps, trim, weight and balance numbers, GPS entries [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]].
Phones and other devices are discouraged during taxi; have everyone turn them off [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(j)]].

callout.text: The briefing trap: you brief the route you expect, then ATC gives you a different one. Follow the clearance or instructions you actually receive, not the ones you expected [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2) CAUTION]].

body.p: Passengers are part of the plan. Remind them about a sterile cockpit, but ask them to speak up if they see a conflict [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(b)]]. With no door between cockpit and cabin, ask them to avoid unnecessary talk from the start of preflight until you reach cruising altitude, and again from landing preparation until you are stopped at the ramp [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]].

Write it down. When taxi instructions are complex or the airport is new to you, copy them in full; on a short, familiar route the basic elements may be enough [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e(1)]]. The AC shows a shorthand:

head: ATC says
You write
rows: "N123 taxi 9R via Bravo, Echo, Juliet, hold short 4L at Echo"
9R B E J 4L E, with the clearance limit (4L at E) circled [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e(2)]]

check.q: In the AC 91-73B shorthand, what does a slash in your written taxi route mean, and what do you circle?
check.a: The slash marks a hold short; you circle the clearance limit [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e(2)]].

chunks.title: Heads up while moving: the continuous loop

body.p: AC 91-73B describes taxi awareness as a continuous loop: know exactly where you are now, and the next spot that will need extra attention, such as a turn onto another taxiway, an intersecting runway or a hot spot [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7d]].

bullets: Keep the airport diagram out and check the assigned route against the heading indicator or compass, especially at complex intersections [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7d(1)]] and where two runways' departure ends are close together [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(1)]].
Do heads-down work before you taxi. Many pilot errors happen while a pilot is off frequency or programming a GPS [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(3) NOTE]].

Read back the runway assignment, any clearance to enter a specific runway, and any instruction to hold short of a runway or line up and wait [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]]. Include your full call sign and the runway, and do not answer these with "Roger" or "Wilco" [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(4)]].
Many runway incursions happen even after a correct hold short readback. Use a physical reminder, such as something placed on an instrument knob or hung on the compass or yoke [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(3)]].

Before entering or crossing any runway, be positive you are cleared, scan the full length of the runway and the final approach, and if anything is unclear, stop and ask ATC [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(4)]]. Scan even when ATC has cleared you [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]].
Listen for similar call signs so you do not act on another aircraft's clearance [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(6)]].

callout.text: Unsure where you are? Do not stop on a runway. Stop the airplane, tell ATC right away and ask for progressive taxi if needed. Runways have white, segmented centerlines; taxiways have continuous yellow ones [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]].

body.p: Low visibility raises the risk [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(4)]]. The tower may not be able to see you at all [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19a]]. Give the airplane your full attention while it moves, and hold checklists and nonessential talk until you are stopped with the brakes set [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19d]].

Once cleared onto the active runway for departure, a single pilot should monitor only ATC frequencies until clear of the Class B, C or D surface area. Do the same from landing clearance until the landing and taxi are complete [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18b2]].

check.q: You read back "hold short of Runway 4" correctly, then got busy. What does AC 91-73B suggest so you do not roll through the line?
check.a: A physical reminder, such as an object on an instrument knob or hung on the compass or yoke [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(3)]].

chunks.title: Lining up: right runway, right clearance

callout.text: At an airport with an operating control tower, no one may operate on a runway or taxiway, or take off or land, without an appropriate ATC clearance [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]]. A taxi instruction to an assigned runway does not authorize entering or crossing that runway at any point [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a6]].

body.p: "Line up and wait" means taxi onto the departure runway, line up and wait. It is not a takeoff clearance. FAA reviews found that a significant number of pilots read back LUAW correctly and then departed without a takeoff clearance [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5a]].

bullets: If ATC gave a reason for the wait, or the reason is plain to see, expect takeoff clearance once it is resolved. If no clearance comes within a reasonable time, call ATC [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5b, c]]. In the accidents and incidents the FAA studied, two minutes or more passed between the LUAW instruction and the event [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5c NOTE]].
Before and while taxiing on, scan the full runway for aircraft crossing it, on final, or on landing roll, including on intersecting runways [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5e]].
If you are not sure a takeoff clearance was for you, ask before you roll [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5f]].

Lights: when entering the runway, turn on all lights except landing lights; turn the landing lights on when cleared for takeoff, or when starting the roll at a non-towered airport [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(d), (f)]]. At night in LUAW, consider lining up about 3 ft left or right of centerline so a landing pilot can tell you apart from the runway lights [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(e)]].

body.p: Runway confusion is a kind of runway incursion that often ends with a takeoff or landing on a taxiway or the wrong runway, usually without the pilot noticing until afterward [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. Three things raise the risk: a complex airport, runway thresholds close together, and a runway used as a taxiway [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. The PHAK cites an August 2006 regional jet cleared for Runway 22 that lined up on shorter Runway 26 and crashed off the end [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

callout.text: Set the heading bug to the runway heading. Before adding power, make one last instrument check that the airplane's heading matches the runway heading [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

body.p: At a non-towered airport, or one whose tower is closed, not every aircraft has a radio. Listen on the CTAF and scan the full runway and its approach and departure paths before entering or crossing [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(12)]]. Do not sit lined up on the departure runway any longer than absolutely necessary [[7:14|AC 91-73B App 1, 5]]. At part-time towers, be certain whether the tower is open before you operate [[7:13|AC 91-73B App 1, 2a]].

check.q: You are in LUAW at night. Time passes, no word from the tower, and the frequency is oddly quiet. What do you do?
check.a: Call ATC; with no clearance after a reasonable time the AIM says to contact them [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5c]]. AC 91-73B adds: if the radio is unusually quiet, suspect a radio problem or stuck microphone and look for light gun signals [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(9) NOTE]].

chunks.title: After landing: clear the runway first, chores second

body.p: Plan the exit before you land. After getting the ATIS, review the airport diagram and brief your exit taxiway, any hold markings close to it, and the rule that you do not cross hold markings or exit onto a runway without ATC clearance [[1:369|PHAK 14-35]].

callout.text: AIM 4-3-21: exit without delay at the first available taxiway or where ATC tells you. Do not exit onto another runway unless ATC authorizes it. At a towered airport, do not stop or reverse course on the runway without ATC approval [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21a]].

body.p: You are not clear of the runway until all parts of the airplane have crossed the holding position marking [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a1]]. Without other ATC instructions, taxi beyond the landing runway's holding position markings, then hold unless ATC has given more instructions [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21b]]. Make sure the tail is across too. If a parallel runway's hold short line keeps you from clearing, stop and tell ATC at once [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(11)]].

bullets: Change nothing (flaps, trim, radios) until the whole airplane has crossed the landing runway's hold short line [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]] [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]].
Do not accept a last-minute turnoff instruction unless you clearly understand it and are certain you can comply safely [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(14)]].
Take extra care after landing on a runway that intersects another one, or where the exit taxiway is close to another runway's hold short line [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(10)]].
Ground's taxi clearance to parking does not authorize entering or crossing any runway [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21c NOTE 2]].

check.q: After landing, when does AC 91-73B say you may raise the flaps and change frequencies?
check.a: Only after the entire airplane has crossed the landing runway's hold short line [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]] [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]].

chunks.title: Landing distance: the book number and the real number

callout.text: 91.103(b): before any flight, the PIC must become familiar with runway lengths at airports of intended use and with takeoff and landing distance information: the AFM data where an approved AFM with that data is required, otherwise other reliable information for the expected elevation, runway slope, gross weight, wind and temperature [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].

body.p: Start with what the chart assumes. Performance charts typically assume a paved, level, smooth and dry runway [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. Then check the length you really have: where no declared distances are published, assume the physical length, except that a displaced threshold shortens the Landing Distance Available [[33:246|AIM 4-3-6d]].

Part 91 has no rule like the airline landing margins, but AC 91-79B recommends that Part 91 pilots calculate landing distance before departure from their AFM data [[27:12|AC 91-79B 2.1.4]]. It also strongly recommends a time of arrival assessment before landing, and explains that AFM distances found in certification flight tests come from test pilots using techniques not used in normal flying [[27:13|AC 91-79B 2.2.3]].

head: What changes
Effect on landing distance (rule of thumb)
rows: Crossing the threshold 10 ft above the standard 50 ft
About 21 percent longer for the first 10 knots [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]] [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]
5 percent faster landing speed, 10 percent longer distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]
5,000 ft field instead of sea level
About 16 percent longer, roughly 3.5 percent per 1,000 ft [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]
Touching down past the POH air distance
The book distance may not be reachable at all [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]]

body.p: Light airplane POHs may not give tailwind data. The AC quotes the Cessna 150 and 152 chart note: for tailwinds up to 10 knots, increase distances by 10 percent for each 2 knots [[27:36|AC 91-79B 5.2.9.1]].

The penalties stack. AC 91-79B Figure 5-1 adds them one at a time until a landing planned for a 5,000 ft runway ends past the end [[27:37|AC 91-79B 5-4]]. The PHAK says to work the tailwind increase on the already-increased fast-landing distance, not on the original number [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]].

callout.text: Once you have an operational landing distance, add at least 15 percent (the Table 3-1 factors in the next chunk already include it). Except in an emergency, do not try to land on a runway that fails that test [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]]. For unfamiliar airports, the RMH suggests adding at least 500 ft to your personal minimum runway length [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

check.q: Your POH distance assumes 50 ft over the threshold. You cross at 70 ft. About how much farther will you need?
check.a: About 400 ft: 200 ft for every 10 ft above 50 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].

body.p: A runway is assumed dry unless reported otherwise, usually by ATIS, NOTAM or PIREP [[27:26|AC 91-79B 4.1]]. Airports give a runway condition code for each third of the runway (touchdown, midpoint, rollout) in the direction of landing [[33:251|AIM 4-3-9c]]. Pilots report braking action in words: good, good to medium, medium, medium to poor, poor and nil [[33:250|AIM 4-3-8a]].

head: RwyCC
Example runway conditions
Braking action
rows: Frost; wet (damp, or 1/8 inch or less of water); 1/8 inch or less of slush, dry snow or wet snow
Compacted snow at minus 15 C or colder
Wet runway listed "slippery when wet"; more than 1/8 inch of dry or wet snow; compacted snow warmer than minus 15 C
More than 1/8 inch of water or slush
Wet ice; slush over ice; water over compacted snow; snow over ice

body.p: Table source: the RCAM [[27:24|AC 91-79B Table 3-2]]. Only 1/8 inch of water separates a wet runway (code 5, good) from standing water (code 2, medium to poor), because dynamic hydroplaning may start whenever water is deeper than that [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.6.1]]. With standing water, braking force can drop by up to 77 percent in seconds, and pilots report the airplane feels like it is speeding up [[27:17|AC 91-79B 3.6]]. In moderate or heavy rain on a smooth runway, assume the water may be deeper than 1/8 inch [[27:17|AC 91-79B 3.5.2]].

bullets: Dynamic hydroplaning needs a water film at least 1/10 inch deep. It starts at about 8.6 times the square root of the tire pressure in psi (24 psi gives about 42 knots), and once started can continue to slower speeds [[24:208|AFH 9-37]].

Reverted rubber hydroplaning follows a long locked-wheel skid; steam lifts the tire. Release the brakes, let the wheels spin up, then brake moderately. It can last down to 20 knots or less [[24:208|AFH 9-37]].
Viscous hydroplaning needs a film no more than 1/1,000 inch deep on a smooth surface or rubber deposits, which can be as slick as wet ice [[24:208|AFH 9-37]].

callout.text: If hydroplaning is possible: land on a grooved runway if there is one, touch down as slowly as safety allows, lower the nose and brake moderately. If you feel no deceleration, raise the nose for aerodynamic drag until the brakes work. Brake firmly to just short of a skid and release at the first sign of one. In a crosswind the airplane will weathervane into the wind and slide downwind at the same time [[24:209|AFH 9-38]]. Land into the wind and avoid abrupt control inputs [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

body.p: When the ATIS says "braking action advisories are in effect," ATC gives every arrival the latest braking report for the runway. Ask for it if you do not get it, and be ready to report the runway after landing [[33:250|AIM 4-3-8c, d]]. If you have not been trained on the in-between terms, report the lowest level you saw [[27:31|AC 91-79B 4.8.3]]. A tailwind on a slippery runway makes an overrun more likely [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.7]].

Table 3-1 of AC 91-79B is a time of arrival tool. When the manufacturer or a performance data provider gives no advisory data for the runway condition, multiply the AFM/POH dry, unfactored landing distance by the landing distance factor (LDF) for the conditions on arrival [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]] [[27:16|AC 91-79B 3.3.3]]. The reciprocating row is 1.67 dry, 2.3 wet grooved or PFC, 2.6 wet smooth, then 2.8, 3.2, 4.0 and 5.1 for codes 4 through 1 [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]. Each factor already includes the 15 percent safety margin plus allowances for normal air distance, approach speed and reduced braking, so do not stack other factors or another 15 percent on top of it [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]].

check.q: The tower reports Runway 27 condition codes 5/5/2. What does the last number tell you?
check.a: The rollout third has more than 1/8 inch of water or slush, medium to poor braking [[33:251|AIM 4-3-9c]] [[27:24|AC 91-79B Table 3-2]].

body.p: A stabilized approach keeps a constant-angle glide path to a chosen point on the runway, at a constant final descent airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. On a stabilized approach the aiming point does not move in the windshield, and the runway keeps the same shape as it grows. If the approach gets shallower the runway looks shorter and wider; if it gets steeper it looks longer and narrower [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

head: AFH element (typical piston airplane)
Stabilized means
rows: Constant, typically 3 degrees to the touchdown zone [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Tracking the centerline with only small corrections; bank normally no more than 15 degrees on final [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Within +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed (AFM, 1.3 VSO, or placard); with a gust factor, never below the recommended speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Landing flaps as required, gear down, in trim [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Generally 500 to 1,000 fpm; if more than 500 fpm, reduce it before 300 ft AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Right for the configuration, not below the AFM minimum for approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Done before the approach, except the landing checklist [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]

callout.text: The gates: stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation in VMC, 1,000 ft in IMC. In the traffic pattern, an approach that becomes unstabilized below 300 ft AGL means an immediate go-around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: Fix small errors early so late corrections stay small [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. If low, add power and raise the nose together. Do not raise the flaps to fix an undershoot; that can cause a sudden loss of lift and a high sink rate [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Stretching a glide with pitch alone is almost always a bad idea [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. For a short field, start final at least 500 ft above the touchdown area and fly no faster than 1.3 VSO when the maker gives no speed, adding no more than half the gust factor; extra speed lands you long [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

AC 91-79B lists the unstabilized approach first among overrun hazards. It also says it is the pilot's job to tell ATC when following an instruction would make the approach unstable because of speed or descent rate [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.1]].

check.q: VMC, a normal pattern. At 400 ft AGL on final you are 15 knots fast and well above the glide path. What does the AFH guidance call for?
check.a: A go-around. You were not stabilized by 500 ft above the airport, and +15 knots is outside +10/-5 KIAS [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: The AFH calls the go-around a normal maneuver for when the approach or landing differs from what you expected or when continuing is hazardous. Any approach may end in one, and the idea that a go-around always means a poor approach or poor skill is a fallacy [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

head: Go around when
Source
rows: You are not stabilized at the gate, or the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 ft AGL in the pattern
You have any doubt the approach can be completed safely, or you are too slow and too low
You cannot touch down in the first third of the runway, or the airplane drifts sideways
You balloon excessively, bounce hard, or porpoising is severe or getting worse
The runway is occupied, even if you have a landing clearance
You doubt you are lined up on the right surface
The turn to final would create a collision hazard, or you are rushing a steep turn to final
ATC requires it, a hazard appears on the runway, wind shear, wake turbulence, or a mechanical failure

body.p: At a towered field, if you are on final without a landing clearance, AC 91-73B tells flight schools to teach: ask the tower "am I cleared to land?" and if there is no answer, go around [[7:18|AC 91-73B App 3, 10]]. A land and hold short (LAHSO) clearance never rules out a rejected landing; if you go around, keep clear of other traffic and tell the controller promptly [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11b5, 6]].

The figure shows a retractable twin; the order is the same for a fixed-gear single, minus the gear. Power comes first, then attitude, then configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Apply full power smoothly, carburetor heat off if applicable, hold the nose down against the trim with forward pressure and right rudder, and bring the flaps up in steps once the descent has stopped [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Ground effect performance is borrowed, so do not try to climb out of it too early [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. On the upwind leg, a shallow turn to the upwind side keeps the runway and departing traffic in view [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. (Handling and loss of control in the go-around are covered in RF.VI.B.)

callout.text: The go-around is not dangerous in itself. It becomes dangerous only when delayed too long or flown badly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

check.q: In a gusty crosswind you float past the first third of the runway. What does the AFH say to do?

chunks.title: Risk: pressing on to a short or wet runway

body.p: The AFH names the two reasons pilots delay a go-around: landing expectancy (the belief that the approach is sure to end safely) and pride (the belief that going around admits failure) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. AC 91-79B adds that landing on a contaminated runway combines cognitive bias, changing weather and high workload, under time pressure, which makes errors likely [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12]]. It warns that plan continuation bias must not drive actions against rules and SOPs [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12.2]].

Expectation bias is a wrong assessment that persists despite evidence. The RMH tells of a GA pilot who read the NOTAM and heard the ATIS about a runway closure that had switched to the parallel runway, still saw it the old way, and started an approach to the closed runway [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

The PHAK tells a true overrun story, which it says repeats every year with new pilots. Downwind for one runway in light rain, the pilot accepted a tight change to another runway with a 10 knot tailwind, dove to make it, and at 50 ft was already 1,000 ft down a 3,500 ft runway and about 10 percent fast. The planned 1,600 ft landing now needed about 3,240 ft of the 3,500 ft runway. The brakes locked, the airplane hydroplaned, and the margin was gone [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]. The PHAK's lesson: bad decisions combine, and each correction has to be bigger, until correction is almost impossible [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]].

bullets: Before departure: work out the landing distance for the expected conditions [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]], and know in advance which LAHSO combinations, if any, you could accept [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11b4]].

Before descent: do the time of arrival assessment, including how much worse the field can get before you divert, so a late bad report gets a quick decision [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.1]]. Brief the worst braking you will accept and what it would look like [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12.3]]. Pilots who operate on their own, with no operator or dispatcher, should map out these decision points before the flight [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3]].
In the terminal area, fly the briefed plan instead of analyzing the risk again [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12.1]].

A late runway change cancels your assessment: confirm the new runway, wind and other factors before you accept [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.11]]. If you cannot comply safely, say "unable" [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]]. The PIC may decline any LAHSO clearance [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11b3]].
Set personal minimums, including a minimum runway length, on the ground; do not adjust them to finish a particular flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

callout.text: Get-there-itis: a fixation on the original goal or destination combined with ignoring other options [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]. Application: on short final to a short wet runway, it sounds like "I'm almost down."

check.q: When does AC 91-79B want you to decide the worst braking action you will accept?
check.a: Before the descent, as part of a briefing; once descending, monitor and respond with the briefed actions [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12.3]].

bullets: Following the taxi route you expected. Fix: follow the instruction you received, and ask if unsure [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2) CAUTION]].
Programming the GPS while rolling. Fix: do heads-down tasks before taxi or when stopped [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(3) NOTE]].
Treating "line up and wait" as a takeoff clearance. Fix: wait for "cleared for takeoff" [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5a]].
Raising flaps while the tail is still over the hold markings. Fix: clear the line completely first [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]].

Planning from the POH number alone on a wet runway. Fix: multiply the dry, unfactored POH number by the Table 3-1 factor, which already includes the margin [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]] [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]].
Accepting a late runway change with a tailwind. Fix: reassess or say "unable" [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.11]] [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].
Saving a high, fast approach with a dive. Fix: go around if not stabilized at the gate [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
Floating down the runway hoping to stop. Fix: go around if you cannot touch down in the first third [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].
Locking the brakes on a wet runway. Fix: release, let the wheels spin up, brake just short of a skid [[24:209|AFH 9-38]].

body.p: Land or go around, in one line each (application, built from the sources above): before descent, decide if the runway passes with margin [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]]; at the gate, decide if you are stabilized [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]; over the runway, decide if you will touch down in the first third [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. Any "no" is a go-around or a diversion.

check.q: What three decision points does this lesson use for "land or go around"?
check.a: Before descent: does the runway pass with margin [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]]. At the gate: stabilized or not [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Over the runway: touchdown in the first third [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

scenario.title: Rain at Riverside
scenario.setup: You fly a Piper Archer to Riverside, a towered airport you have never visited, to meet a client. Runway 27 is 4,000 ft, smooth (not grooved). Runway 33 is 2,800 ft and crosses Runway 27 near its middle. Your POH landing distance over a 50 ft obstacle is 1,150 ft for today's weight and temperature, for a dry runway with no margin added, and the POH has no data for wet runways. A line of rain showers is moving through. The ATIS says: wind 090 at 8, Runway 27 in use, braking action advisories in effect, Runway 27 condition codes 5/5/2.

questions.q: Before you left home, besides the runway lengths and landing distance data 91.103 requires, what should you have mapped out for Riverside?
questions.a: 91.103(b) covers the runway lengths and your landing distance information for the expected conditions [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]. AC 91-79B adds that pilots who operate on their own should map out their time of arrival decision points before the flight [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3]], including how much worse the field can get before they divert [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.1]]. Application: with showers forecast, that means knowing the condition code that makes you hold or divert, and where you would go.

questions.q: Using AC 91-79B Table 3-1, what landing distance do the codes 5/5/2 call for, and does Runway 27 work?
questions.a: Use the most adverse reliable report or condition for the part of the runway you will use [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.3]]. Multiply the dry, unfactored POH distance by the reciprocating code 2 factor: 1,150 x 4.0 = 4,600 ft, more than the 4,000 ft available. The factor already includes the 15 percent margin, so nothing more is added [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]] [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]. The wind from 090 is also a tailwind on Runway 27, which makes an overrun on a slippery runway more likely [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.7]]. Application: hold or divert until the water drains or a better runway is offered.

questions.q: After the shower passes, the codes are 5/5/5 on both runways and the wind is calm. Tower then offers "short approach, Runway 33, cleared to land" to save time. What do you consider?
questions.a: A runway change means your assessment no longer applies; confirm the runway, wind and other factors before accepting [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.11]]. Code 5 on a smooth runway is factor 2.6: 1,150 x 2.6 = 2,990 ft [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]. That fits Runway 27 (4,000 ft) but not Runway 33 (2,800 ft). Say "unable" if you cannot safely comply [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].

questions.q: On final for Runway 27 you get gusts. At 400 ft AGL you are 14 knots above your target speed and sinking 1,100 fpm. Continue?
questions.a: No. You are past the 500 ft VMC gate and outside +10/-5 KIAS, and the descent rate is above what the AFH lists [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Go around: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

questions.q: On the second approach you land on Runway 27. As you slow, the nearest paved turnoff is Runway 33, crossing just ahead; taxiway Alpha 3 is beyond it. The tower has said nothing about Runway 33. What do you do?
questions.a: Do not exit onto Runway 33 unless ATC authorizes it, and do not stop or reverse course on the runway without approval; exit at the first available taxiway or where ATC tells you [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21a]]. Take extra care landing on a runway that intersects another [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(10)]]. Once every part of the airplane is past Alpha 3's hold markings, hold unless told otherwise, and change nothing until then [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21b]] [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]].

questions.q: Next morning in fog you must cross Runway 33 to reach Runway 27. How do you set up the taxi?
questions.a: Review NOTAMs, the diagram and hot spots, and brief the route and runway crossing before moving [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b(1)]] [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(d)]]. Write down and read back the instructions, including the hold short [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e(1)]] [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]]. In low visibility the tower may not see you: keep checklists for when you are stopped with brakes set, and tell ATC at once if you become disoriented [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19]].

skills.do: Given an approach situation (runway length and condition, wind, your speed, height and where you will touch down), decide whether to land or go around and explain why using three checks: does the runway pass a landing distance assessment with margin, are you stabilized at the gate, and will you touch down in the first third of the runway.
skills.practice: On the ground, take your POH dry, unfactored landing distance and multiply it by the AC 91-79B Table 3-1 factors for a wet and a code 2 runway (the factors already include the 15 percent margin) [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]] [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]], and write down your go-around triggers [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. In flight with a CFI, call "stable" or "go around" aloud at 500 ft and 300 ft AGL, and fly at least two planned go-arounds from short final [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: Per AC 91-73B, when should you run pre-departure checklists, if possible?
options: While crossing a runway, so the checklist is finished before reaching the run-up area
Whenever ground control is silent, since a quiet frequency means no traffic conflicts
Only when stopped or taxiing straight ahead with no complex intersections
Only during the run-up, and never earlier, so all other taxi time is kept free
quiz.why: If possible, run them only when stopped or taxiing straight ahead with no complex intersections [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]].

quiz.q: Ground clears you to taxi via Taxiway Charlie, but a NOTAM says Charlie is closed. What does AC 91-73B say to do?
options: Taxi via Charlie; ATC knows best
Query the controller to verify the clearance
Pick a different taxiway yourself
Cancel the flight
quiz.why: If ATC clears you onto a surface that a NOTAM or the ATIS shows closed, query the controller for verification [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b(1)(c)]].

quiz.q: Tower says "N52TX, Runway 24, line up and wait." What are you authorized to do?
options: Take off after 90 seconds if you hear nothing
Take off when traffic is clear
Hold short of Runway 24
Taxi onto Runway 24, line up and wait
quiz.why: LUAW tells you to taxi onto the departure runway, line up and wait. It is not an authorization to take off [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5a]].

quiz.q: You are a single pilot, just cleared onto the active runway at a Class D airport. Until you leave the Class D surface area, what should you listen to?
options: Only ATC communications
ATIS, to catch any update
Ground control and tower together
Any frequency, as long as you scan outside
quiz.why: A single pilot should monitor only assigned ATC communications after being cleared onto the active runway, until clear of the Class B, C or D surface area [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18b2]].

quiz.q: You land 10 percent heavier than the weight in your usual POH example. About how much longer is the minimum landing distance?
options: About 5 percent
About 50 percent
About 21 percent
About 10 percent
quiz.why: A 10 percent increase in landing weight gives about a 5 percent faster landing speed and a 10 percent longer landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]] [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.6]].

quiz.q: According to AC 91-79B, what can happen to braking when standing water lifts the tires?
options: Braking force can drop by up to 77 percent within seconds, and the airplane may feel like it speeds up
Braking drops slowly over several hundred feet, so there is time to react and correct
Only directional control is affected, while braking stays at its normal strength and the airplane stops as planned
Braking improves as soon as the tires cut through the water, so brake harder at first
quiz.why: With standing water, braking can degrade in seconds, by up to 77 percent, and pilots report the airplane feels like it accelerates; cornering suffers too [[27:17|AC 91-79B 3.6]].

quiz.q: An airport reports three runway condition codes for your runway. What do they describe?
options: Braking action as reported by the last three pilots to land on that runway
Left edge, centerline and right edge of the runway, as seen from the threshold
Morning, midday and evening inspections by airport operations, in that order
The touchdown, midpoint and rollout zones, in the direction of landing
quiz.why: Runway condition codes are given for each zone (touchdown, mid-point, roll-out), in the direction of takeoff and landing [[33:251|AIM 4-3-9c]].

quiz.q: For a typical piston airplane, what airspeed band does the AFH call stabilized on final?
options: Any speed above 1.1 VSO, as long as the flaps are fully extended
Within 5 knots either way of VY with the flaps set for landing
Within +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed
Within +20/-10 KIAS of normal cruise speed, adjusted for the wind
quiz.why: Within +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed in the AFM, 1.3 VSO, or on placards [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, when does a go-around become dangerous?
options: Only when it is delayed unduly or done improperly
Whenever it starts below 300 ft
Whenever the airplane has full flaps set
Whenever ATC did not ask for it
quiz.why: The go-around is not dangerous in itself; it becomes dangerous only when delayed unduly or executed improperly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: Two runway thresholds sit side by side at the end of your taxiway, Runway 36 and Runway 4. You are cleared for takeoff on Runway 36. What is your last check before adding power?
options: Confirm the heading indicator agrees with the runway heading, about 360
Check the oil temperature
Call ground control for confirmation
Look for the wind sock
final_quiz.why: Set the heading bug to the runway heading and, before adding power, make one last instrument scan to be sure the airplane heading and runway heading agree [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

final_quiz.q: At night you are told to line up and wait on a runway with landing traffic behind you. How should your lights be set?
options: All lights off, to avoid blinding the pilot of the landing airplane behind you
Only the beacon on, since the strobes and landing light would blind the traffic behind
Landing lights only, so the pilot behind can see where your airplane is on the runway
All lights except landing lights, then landing lights on at takeoff clearance
final_quiz.why: On entering the runway for takeoff or LUAW, turn on all lights except landing lights; turn landing lights on when takeoff clearance is received [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(d), (f)]].

final_quiz.q: At a non-towered airport you are ready for takeoff, but an airplane is still on the runway after landing. What does AC 91-73B say about lining up now so you are ready?
options: Line up and hold; it shows other traffic at the field that you are ready for an immediate takeoff
Lining up to wait is only allowed at night, when the airplane's lights can be seen
Line up and hold with the strobes on, as long as you announce it on the CTAF first
Do not line up on the departure runway and hold any longer than absolutely necessary
final_quiz.why: At airports without an operating tower, do not line up on the departure runway and hold any longer than absolutely necessary; some aircraft there may have no radio [[7:14|AC 91-73B App 1, 5]].

final_quiz.q: Taxiing in fog with RVR about 1,000 ft, you need to load a new flight plan in the GPS. When?
options: Now, while taxiing slowly
At the hold short line while still rolling
Only when stopped with the brakes set
During the takeoff roll
final_quiz.why: In low visibility, checklists and nonessential tasks wait until the aircraft is stopped and the brakes set [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19d]]; heads-down tasks are done while stopped [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(4)]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH gives 1,100 ft to land over 50 ft, dry, with no margin added. The runway is wet and grooved (code 5), and there is no other data. Which plan follows AC 91-79B Table 3-1?
options: 1,100 x 2.3 = 2,530 ft, with nothing added
1,100 x 2.6 = 2,860 ft, since every wet runway uses the smooth factor
1,100 x 2.3 = 2,530 ft, plus 15 percent = 2,910 ft
final_quiz.why: Multiply the dry, unfactored AFM/POH distance by the factor; the factors already include the 15 percent margin, so adding it again double counts [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]]. Wet grooved (code 5) reciprocating is 2.3: 1,100 x 2.3 = 2,530 ft; 2.6 is for a smooth runway [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]].

final_quiz.q: You arrive at an airport. The ATIS mentions no runway condition, and there is no NOTAM or PIREP about it. How does AC 91-79B treat the runway?
options: As wet, to be safe, since an unreported surface may be damp from dew or earlier rain
As code 5, the typical condition for a wet runway when nothing has been reported
As unknown, so you may not land until the airport operator issues a condition report
As dry, since a runway is assumed dry unless reported otherwise
final_quiz.why: A runway is assumed dry unless reported otherwise, usually through the ATIS, NOTAM or PIREP [[27:26|AC 91-79B 4.1]]. Application: still watch the weather, because conditions can change faster than the reports [[27:16|AC 91-79B 3.4.1]].

final_quiz.q: You touch down on a wet runway and brake, but feel no deceleration; you suspect dynamic hydroplaning. What does the AFH recommend?
options: Pump the brakes rapidly so the tires break through the water film and grip
Hold full brakes until the airplane stops, since braking will start to work eventually
Raise the nose and use aerodynamic drag until the brakes become effective
Add power and steer with the brakes to keep the airplane tracking the centerline
final_quiz.why: If deceleration is not felt and hydroplaning is suspected, raise the nose and use aerodynamic drag until the brakes become effective; brake to just short of a skid [[24:209|AFH 9-38]].

final_quiz.q: At night, on final to an unfamiliar airport, you are not sure the lighted surface ahead is the runway you were cleared to. What does the AFH say to do?
options: Continue and check the runway number after touchdown
Go around and consider the situation further
Land; the tower would have warned you
Descend lower to read the markings
final_quiz.why: Verify runway alignment and number on final; if there is a doubt over the landing surface, go around and consider the situation further [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

final_quiz.q: Cleared to land, on short final, you see an airplane holding in position on your runway. What should you do?
options: Land long and stop behind the airplane holding, since your landing clearance is valid
Do not land on an occupied runway: ask the controller and be ready to go around
Land as cleared; you have a landing clearance, so the controller is responsible
Land on the parallel taxiway, which is clear, and report the event after landing
final_quiz.why: Never land on a runway occupied by another aircraft, even with a landing clearance. Ask the controller and be prepared to go around [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5i]].

final_quiz.q: At a towered airport you are on short final and realize you never heard a landing clearance. The tower is busy. What does AC 91-73B tell flight schools to teach?
options: Ask the tower "am I cleared to land?" and if there is no answer, go around
Land; the tower expects you and would have told you if landing was not allowed
Rock your wings to get the controller's attention, then land if the tower does not respond
Switch to ground control and ask whether you are cleared to land on the runway
final_quiz.why: Ask the tower, "(call sign), am I cleared to land?" and if there is no response, execute a go-around [[7:18|AC 91-73B App 3, 10]]. A clearance is required to land at a towered airport [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]].

final_quiz.q: A runway is 4,000 ft long, has a 600 ft displaced landing threshold, and has no published declared distances. Your time of arrival check gives 3,500 ft. Can you accept it?
options: Yes, 3,500 ft is less than 4,000 ft
No; the landing distance available is 3,400 ft
Yes, you may land on the displaced part
Only if the tower approves
final_quiz.why: Without published declared distances, assume the physical length, but a displaced landing threshold shortens the LDA by its length: 4,000 - 600 = 3,400 ft [[33:246|AIM 4-3-6d]]. Your required distance must fall within the declared distances before you accept the runway [[33:246|AIM 4-3-6d]].

final_quiz.q: Your destination runs land and hold short (LAHSO) operations. According to the AIM, when should you work out which LAHSO combinations you could accept?
options: When the tower offers one on final, using the distance remaining on the runway
Only if you are a student pilot, since only student pilots are required to plan ahead for LAHSO
During preflight planning, using your airplane's landing distance and the published ALD
After landing, using the roll-out distance you actually used, to plan the next flight
final_quiz.why: Preflight planning should include an assessment of which LAHSO combinations work for your airplane's required landing distance, using the published Available Landing Distance; good decision making is knowing in advance whether you can accept one [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11b4]].

final_quiz.q: On final you are a little low and short of your aiming point. Which correction does the AFH warn against?
options: Adding power while raising the nose slightly
Leveling off briefly with power to rejoin the glide path
Retracting the flaps to reduce the descent
Glancing at the airspeed
final_quiz.why: Retracting flaps to fix an undershoot can cause a sudden loss of lift and an excessive sink rate; add power and raise the nose instead [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

takeaways: Plan and brief the taxi like any phase of flight, and follow the clearance you get, not the one you expected.
Heads-down tasks happen before taxi or when stopped; read back hold short instructions and set a reminder.
Line up and wait is not a takeoff clearance; check the heading against the runway before adding power.
After landing, clear the hold markings with the whole airplane before touching flaps or radios.
Book landing distance is a best case: fast, high, tailwind, slope and wet runways stack up, so add margin.
Know the gates: stabilized by 500 ft (VMC), go around if unstable below 300 ft or if you cannot land in the first third.
Decide your limits before descent; in the terminal area, fly the plan and go around without debate.
cfi_notes: AC 91-73B 7d(9) and Appendix 3 item 9 say to expect ATC to call within 90 seconds of a LUAW instruction [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(9)]] [[7:18|AC 91-73B App 3, 9]], and PHAK 14-35 says to contact ATC if no takeoff clearance comes within 90 seconds [[1:369|PHAK 14-35]]. The current AIM says to contact ATC if takeoff clearance is not received "within a reasonable amount of time" and notes that two minutes or more passed in the events the FAA studied [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5c]] [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5c NOTE]]. This lesson teaches the AIM wording.

AC 91-73B 7f(4) says pilots are "required to read back all clearances" [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(4)]], and PHAK 14-32 calls a verbatim hold short readback "mandatory" [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. The AIM says pilots should always read back the runway assignment, clearances to enter a runway, and hold short or LUAW instructions, and that controllers must obtain the hold short readback [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9, a10, b1 NOTE]]. 91.123 requires compliance with clearances but has no readback wording [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]]. Interpretation: teach the AIM list and treat readback as required in practice.

Hydroplaning numbers differ: AFH 9-37 uses 8.6 x square root of tire pressure and a water film of at least 1/10 inch [[24:208|AFH 9-37]]; PHAK 11-14 rounds to 9 x square root [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]; AC 91-79B uses more than 1/8 inch as the point where hydroplaning may start [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.6.1]]. Teach them as approximations, not limits.

PHAK 11-17 says a 10 percent excess landing speed causes "at least a 21 percent" increase in landing distance, then a few lines later says 20 percent [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. AC 91-79B uses 20 percent [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]]. PHAK 11-18 also uses "20 percent for every ten miles per hour" of wind, and says to compute it on the already-increased distance, yet its own 320 ft is 20 percent of the original 1,600 ft [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]. PHAK 11-17 and AC 91-79B give about 21 percent for a 10 knot tailwind [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]] [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]]. This lesson uses the AC numbers and multiplies each step on the new number.

AC 91-79B says its braking risks are mostly linked with transport category aircraft and that its guidance may be used by other aircraft with similar designs [[27:5|AC 91-79B 1.6.1]], and there are no plans to give Part 23 makers advisory data like AC 25-32 [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.3]]. Table 3-1 has a reciprocating row, meant for a time of arrival check when no manufacturer or data-provider advisory data exists, applied to the dry, unfactored AFM/POH distance, and it already includes the 15 percent margin [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]] [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]. The AC does not say the factors were built for light singles, and its operational data usually assumes 1,500 ft or 7 seconds of air distance [[27:19|AC 91-79B 3.9]], far more than a short-field landing. Teach them as conservative margins, have pilots compare them with their POH, and do not let anyone stack them with the Figure 5-1 hazard percentages or a second 15 percent.

AIM 4-3-9 still points to "AC 91-79, Mitigating the Risks of a Runway Overrun Upon Landing, Appendix 1" for the RCAM terms [[33:251|AIM 4-3-9]]. AC 91-79B canceled AC 91-79A with that title [[27:4|AC 91-79B 1.4]], and the RCAM is now its Table 3-2 [[27:24|AC 91-79B Table 3-2]]. Likewise, AIM 5-2-5 references AC 91-73A [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5 REFERENCE]], which AC 91-73B canceled [[7:1|AC 91-73B 2]].

The 500 ft, 1,000 ft and 300 ft gates are AFH guidance [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]; no Part 91 rule sets go-around criteria. Have the pilot brief their own triggers aloud before each approach, then hold them to it.

AC 91-73B Appendix 3 asks instructors to limit cockpit instruction during taxi and suggests a panel placard as a reminder [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3, 2]]. Model this on the flight review: teach at the run-up, not while crossing runways.

The PHAK's runway incursion figures (about 65 percent pilot caused, about three per day at towered airports) carry no year on the page [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]] [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. Use them to show the size of the problem, not as current statistics.
gaps: Most light-airplane POHs give landing distance only for a paved, level, dry runway; some give little or no guidance for contaminated runways [[30:25|RMH 3-7]] [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. Wet, grass and contaminated corrections for your airplane need the POH/AFM or a CFI.
The braking action examples and reliable-report criteria in AC 91-79B are built around transport jets with anti-skid; the sources give no light single braking examples.
Tailwind landing data for your airplane, if any, is only in the POH/AFM; the AC quotes just the Cessna 150/152 and TBM 850 notes.
Airport-specific hot spots, declared distances, LAHSO Available Landing Distances and arresting systems come from the airport diagram and Chart Supplement, not from these sources.
The sources do not say how a light airplane behaves in an EMAS bed; the PHAK describes it for overruns in general.

activities.title: True or false: the single-pilot taxi
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: AC 91-73B says to plan the airport surface movement as part of flight planning, like any other phase of flight.
cards.why: True. Plan surface movement just as you plan the other phases of flight [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b]].

cards.s: AC 91-73B says phones are fine during taxi as long as the pilot is not the one using them.
cards.why: False. Phones and other devices are discouraged during taxi, and everyone aboard should turn them off to prevent distractions [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(j)]].

cards.s: One taxi briefing before engine start covers the whole flight, including the taxi in after landing.
cards.why: False. Brief when the items are relevant and fresh: before taxi and again before the initial descent to land [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b(2)]].

cards.s: Taxi instructions to your departure runway let you cross that same runway wherever your route meets it.
cards.why: False. They do not authorize entering or crossing the assigned departure runway at any point [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a6]].

cards.s: Runways have white, segmented centerlines; taxiways have continuous yellow ones.
cards.why: True. AC 91-73B gives this as a cue when you are unsure where you are [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]].

cards.s: Instructors should limit cockpit instruction while taxiing.
cards.why: True. AC 91-73B asks instructors to limit instruction during critical phases, especially taxiing [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3, 2]].

activities.title: The landing distance check, in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps of a time of arrival landing distance check in order, then tap Check.
steps: Before the flight, map out your landing decision points and know your POH dry, unfactored landing distance
Before top of descent, get the landing weather and the runway condition reports
Pick the most adverse reliable report or expected condition for the part of the runway you will use
Multiply the dry, unfactored POH distance by the Table 3-1 factor for that condition
Compare the result with the landing distance available
Brief the worst braking you will accept and what you will do if a worse report comes
In the terminal area, fly the briefed plan instead of analyzing again
activities.why: Map decision points before the flight [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3]]. The assessment is first done when weather and field conditions are obtained, usually before top of descent [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.1]], using the most adverse reliable report [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.3]]. Multiply the dry, unfactored distance by the LDF [[27:16|AC 91-79B 3.3.3]], and the result must fit the declared distances [[33:246|AIM 4-3-6d]]. Brief the worst acceptable braking before descent [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12.3]], then in the terminal area execute the briefed plan [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12.1]].

activities.title: Which kind of hydroplaning?
activities.intro: Tap each clue, then tap the type of hydroplaning it describes.

items.t: Needs a water film at least 1/10 inch deep
Starts at about 8.6 x the square root of tire pressure
A wedge of water builds under the tire at high speed
Steam forms and holds the tire off the runway
Fix: release the brakes, let the wheels spin up, brake moderately
Needs a film no more than 1/1,000 inch deep
Needs a smooth surface or a touchdown zone coated with rubber
Can happen at a much lower speed than the high-speed type

activities.why: All from the AFH [[24:208|AFH 9-37]]: dynamic hydroplaning needs at least 1/10 inch of water, a water wedge forms, and it starts near 8.6 x the square root of tire pressure; reverted rubber (steam) follows a prolonged locked-wheel skid, and the fix is to release the brakes, let the wheels spin up and brake moderately; viscous needs only a film no more than 1/1,000 inch on a smooth or rubber-coated surface and can occur at a much lower speed than dynamic.

activities.title: How much runway, really?
activities.intro: Work each one out, then type your answer.

items.q: A Cessna 152 chart shows 1,200 ft. You land with a 6 knot tailwind. Using the chart note quoted in AC 91-79B (10 percent for each 2 knots), what distance?

Your POH dry, unfactored landing distance is 1,180 ft. The runway is wet and grooved (code 5), with no wet data in the POH. Using the reciprocating row of AC 91-79B Table 3-1, what landing distance is required?
items.why: Wet grooved or PFC (code 5) factor 2.3: 1,180 x 2.3 = 2,714 ft [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]. The factor already includes the 15 percent margin, so nothing is added [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]].

items.q: Your POH dry, unfactored landing distance is 1,050 ft. The runway is reported code 3 (medium). Using the reciprocating row of Table 3-1, what landing distance is required?
items.why: Code 3 reciprocating factor 3.2: 1,050 x 3.2 = 3,360 ft, with the 15 percent margin already inside [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]] [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]].

items.q: The landing distance available is 3,920 ft and the runway is code 4. What is the longest POH dry, unfactored landing distance that still passes, using the reciprocating Table 3-1 factor?
items.why: Code 4 reciprocating factor 2.8. Required = POH x 2.8, so the most POH distance that fits is 3,920 / 2.8 = 1,400 ft [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]].

items.q: A different method: start from a dry-runway POH distance of 1,450 ft and add hazards the AC 91-79B Figure 5-1 way. You will be 10 percent fast (plus 20 percent) with a 10 knot tailwind (plus 21 percent, applied on the new number), then add a 15 percent margin. What is the total, to the nearest 5 ft?
items.why: 1,450 x 1.20 = 1,740; 1,740 x 1.21 = 2,105.4; 2,105.4 x 1.15 = 2,421.2, about 2,420 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]] [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]] [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]]. Working each step on the new number follows the PHAK's stated method [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]. This is not the Table 3-1 method; never add these percentages to a Table 3-1 result.

activities.title: Read the runway picture
activities.intro: Drag each label to the view it describes.

pins.label: Too high: runway looks long and narrow
Too low: runway looks short and wide

activities.why: A steeper approach makes the runway look longer and narrower; a shallower one makes it look shorter and wider; on a stabilized approach its shape stays the same [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. The original figure labels the panels too high, proper descent angle and too low [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

activities.title: Name the trap
activities.intro: Tap a thinking trap, then what it means.

pairs.r: Believing the approach is sure to end in a safe landing
Believing a go-around admits you flew the approach badly
A wrong picture that persists despite evidence against it
Pushing aside information that does not fit what you expect
Fixed on the destination, ignoring other options
Unable to recognize and cope with a changing situation

activities.why: Landing expectancy and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Expectation and confirmation bias [[30:45|RMH 6-2]]. Get-there-itis and mind set [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]].

activities.title: Short, wet and tempting
activities.intro: You fly a Cessna 172 to a towered airport in light rain. Runway 31 is 3,800 ft and smooth (not grooved); your POH landing distance is 1,200 ft, dry, with no margin added. You are 25 NM out and about to start down.

steps.s: The ATIS says braking action advisories are in effect, but approach control has not given you a braking report. What now?
options: Wait; the tower will tell you on short final if the braking report matters for your landing
Ask ATC for the braking report, finish your landing distance check, and brief the worst braking you will accept
Plan to land long to stay above the standing water, then brake hard once past it
Give ATC your own braking report before you land, to help the next arrivals
steps.why: With advisories in effect, ATC gives each arrival the latest braking report, and pilots should ask if it is not issued [[33:250|AIM 4-3-8d]]. Do the assessment when field conditions come in, before descent [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.1]], and brief the worst acceptable braking before descent [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12.3]].

steps.s: Tower reports codes 5/5/5 on both runways and offers Runway 4, 2,900 ft and also smooth, with a 10 knot tailwind, to save time. For Runway 31 you worked out code 5 smooth: 1,200 x 2.6 = 3,120 ft. Your answer?
options: Accept; 2,900 ft is plenty for a 172
Accept and use heavy braking
"Unable, request Runway 31"
Accept but fly faster to make it
steps.why: The change voids your assessment [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.11]]. Runway 4 needs the same 3,120 ft and only 2,900 ft is there [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]], and a tailwind on a slippery runway makes an overrun more likely [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.7]]. Say "unable" [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].

steps.s: On a 3 mile final to Runway 31, tower asks you to keep your speed up for faster traffic behind you. Doing it would leave you about 15 knots fast at the 500 ft gate. What do you do?
options: Comply; ATC instructions come first, and you can slow the airplane down later on short final
Comply and slip off the extra speed in the flare to land on the planned touchdown point
Tell tower you are unable, because it would make your approach unstable
Raise the flaps so the airplane can fly faster while the approach stays stable
steps.why: It is the pilot's job to tell ATC when following an instruction would make the approach unstable because of speed [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.1]]. +15 knots is outside +10/-5 KIAS [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], and 10 percent fast adds about 20 percent to the landing distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]]. Say "unable" [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].

steps.s: Second approach is stable, but in the flare a gust makes you float. You pass the first third of the runway still airborne. Now?
options: Go around
Keep floating and brake hard after touchdown
Close the throttle and hope
Push the nose down to force it on
steps.why: If a landing cannot be made on the first third of the runway, go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. Landing beyond the planned touchdown point can make the computed distance unreachable [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]].

steps.s: Third approach: you land on speed in the first third. Braking feels weaker than the reported "good." What do you do after clearing the runway?
options: Nothing; you stopped
Report a runway condition code
Report "good" to keep traffic moving
Tell ATC; braking was worse than reported
steps.why: If braking is worse than reported, report it to ATC to alert other pilots [[27:27|AC 91-79B 4.5.1]]. Pilots report braking action in words, not codes [[27:28|AC 91-79B 4.6.1]].
